extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, and readers interested in the social/ethical aims of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for fiction and history that avoid an exclusively masculine perspective, urging wider subject-matter (social life, motherhood, women's interrelations, post‑marriage life) and truthful representation of human life. Useful for authors and critics aiming to broaden literary themes and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Androcentric/male-dominated bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature has been 'masculized' by men writing and reading as if 'men are people' and women a side-issue; this male monopoly skews subject-matter and perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay explains that because men have been treated as the default 'human,' literature reflects male preoccupations; writers/critics should recognize and correct this bias by broadening whose experiences count as 'human'. Examples/anti-patterns: men's exclusive control of the making of books; the habitual acceptance of masculine canons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of subject-matter (life in its fullness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction should represent 'human life' in its full range — all emotions, processes, and experiences — not arbitrarily select one emotion or process as the necessary base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works on whether they 'take in more than one field' and show a wide range of persons and activities (e.g., Balzac, Dickens praised for breadth). Anti-pattern: stories that restrict themselves to one dominant note or a narrow slice of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusive focus on Love and War
rubrics_metrics.description: The two dominant branches — the Story of Adventure and the Love Story — reflect masculine interests (Desire and Combat) and are overemphasized at the expense of other human processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fiction that treats other human interests and social processes; flag works that imply 'life has no interests except conflict and love' or that editors force 'heart interest' into works where it does not belong.

rubrics_metrics.name: History and fiction should record social/processual life, not only warfare/conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: History 'is, or should be, the story of our racial life' — including arts, trades, religion, commerce, agriculture — not merely the record of wars, conquests and triumphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical writing and historical fiction for inclusion of discoveries, inventions, professions, and everyday social development; treat records of warfare as partial, not total, history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict motherhood and parent-child relations as central subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Mother-love (and father-love, and the long drama of parent-child relationships) should be treated as principal subjects of fiction — not subordinated to lover-love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for sustained, realistic portrayals of motherhood across stages (not only sentimental or perpetual-baby tropes). The author argues 'the mother's love should be the principal subject' because it is a major life-force and educative for social life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray women's interrelations and social roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction should explore 'the interrelation of women' and their social interactions — a field that was previously underrepresented because women were not producers/subjects of literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value narratives that examine friendships, rivalries, mentorships, and institutional relations among women (beyond harems/convents as limited historical examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict long-term life-course (beyond pre-marital struggle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conventional love-story treats the 'pre-marital struggle' and typically 'stops when he gets her' — fiction ought to follow lives across decades and stages (the 'seventy year stretch').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward narratives that show development after marriage, middle age, old age, and the slow changes of character and social position rather than truncating at marriage ('and lived happily ever after').

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic female perspective (not reflexive/male-imposed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Woman's love as currently treated in much fiction is 'largely a reflex' — presented as the way a man expects her to feel, not how she actually feels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess characterization for interior truthfulness to women's experiences rather than stereotyped, male-projected desires. Anti-pattern: female emotions rendered only as responses to male action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction as truthful re-presentation (educative function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction ought to 'teach us life' not by preaching but by 'truly re-presenting' realities so readers can grow acquainted with a broader range of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that impart knowledge of social life through accurate depiction and sympathetic understanding; penalize works that distort life for marketable formulae or moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great artists transcend sex in portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: The best writers 'transcend sex' and represent life broadly; masters (Balzac, Dickens) refuse to be held to masculine canons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transcendence as a quality metric: does the author portray people of both sexes with full humanity and reach beyond sex-limited stereotypes?

rubrics_metrics.name: Include everyday work and domestic labor as worthy literary material
rubrics_metrics.description: Household labor 'calls for the practice of several distinct crafts' and is of 'most vital importance' in maintaining life and health; such domestic work deserves serious representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate realism for attention to material details (hours, crafts, economic calculations) and for treating domestic work as skilled, responsible labor rather than trivial background. Example/illustration: Miss Bell's detailed account of hours, wages, and tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist market/editorial pressure to narrow subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers/marketers and conservative tastes oppose broader fiction on self-interest, demanding familiar 'heart interest' or formulaic attractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work's form/content is shaped by market-driven demands (forced 'heart interest') and favor creative risk-taking that broadens readers' understanding of life.
